analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare and raises federal Medicaid payments for those services.
analysis.headline: The Senate sent the bill to the Finance Committee in March 2023, and it never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make Medicare cover dental care, eyeglasses and eye exams, and hearing exams and hearing aids — services that are largely excluded from traditional Medicare today. It would also raise the federal share of Medicaid payments to 90% when states cover dental, vision, and hearing care for adults. Sponsor Sen. Bob Casey introduced it with five Democratic colleagues in March 2023; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and saw no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who today pay out of pocket for most dental care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids, would gain coverage with set frequency limits (two dental cleanings a year, one eye exam a year, one hearing aid per ear every four years, dentures every five years). Low-income adults on Medicaid in states with limited dental, vision, or hearing coverage would also benefit, because the federal government would pick up 90% of the cost of those services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare and low-income Medicaid adults

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would cover routine dental cleanings and exams, fillings, crowns, root canals, extractions, emergency dental care, and dentures — services currently excluded from traditional Medicare [S2].
Medicare would cover routine eye exams, eyeglasses, contact lenses, and low-vision devices, and routine hearing exams and hearing aids, which the Medicare statute currently excludes [S3].

The federal Medicaid matching rate would rise to 90% for state spending on dental, vision, and hearing services for adults, making it cheaper for states to cover these services for low-income adults [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and taxpayers would pay the cost of the new Medicare benefits and the higher Medicaid matching rate. The bill contains no financing or offset provisions of its own, so the added spending would come from the general Treasury. Beneficiaries would also bear part of the cost during a long phase-in: Medicare's share of dental, vision, and hearing payments starts at 0% in the first year and climbs 10 points a year until it reaches 80% in the eighth year [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, and beneficiaries during phase-in

drawbacks.text: The bill has no dedicated financing: it adds major new Medicare and Medicaid entitlements without revenue or offsets, so the cost would add to federal deficits unless Congress funded it separately.

Coverage phases in slowly. Medicare would pay 0% of dental, vision, and hearing costs in the first year, rising 10 percentage points annually to 80% by the eighth year, meaning beneficiaries would still face most costs for years after enactment [S3].

The benefit is capped: two dental cleanings and exams per year, one eye exam per year, contact lenses limited to $200 per two years, one hearing aid per ear every four years, and one set of dentures every five years [S3].
The Health and Human Services Secretary could impose additional limits or prior-authorization requirements on any of the new services [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses real, well-documented gaps: traditional Medicare has excluded routine dental care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids since 1965, and many low-income adults live in states with little Medicaid dental coverage. The honest cost is money — a large new open-ended federal entitlement with no financing attached — plus a design weakness in the eight-year phase-in that delays the benefit for the people it is meant to help. The coverage limits are reasonable for a first benefit but tight, particularly the $200 contact-lens cap and the five-year denture limit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2023, and the committee never acted on it, so it never reached the floor before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey and five Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on March 16, 2023 [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the bill's only action of record in the entire Congress [S5].
No committee vote, markup, or Senate floor vote ever occurred, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without further action [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything from the bill's death; the main effect is that the status quo persisted. Medicare Advantage insurers keep the dental, vision, and hearing supplements they market to attract enrollees, and Medicare beneficiaries and Medicaid adults continue to pay out of pocket or go without dental, vision, and hearing care.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo holders; seniors still pay out of pocket

for.name: Sens. Cardin, Brown, Blumenthal, Fetterman, and Welch
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate Finance Committee / Chairman Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The committee took no action — no markup, no vote — on the bill during the entire 118th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican joined; with a committee majority able to block action, a bill with no Republican support had no path to a floor vote.

industries.note: A new Medicare dental benefit would create a paying payer for cleanings, fillings, root canals, and dentures for tens of millions of seniors — new revenue that runs directly alongside patients getting care they currently skip.
Medicare coverage of hearing exams and hearing aids would open a large publicly funded market, while giving seniors access to devices that commonly cost thousands of dollars out of pocket.

industries.industry: Optometrists, optical retailers, and eyewear makers
industries.note: Coverage of eye exams, eyeglasses, and contact lenses would route new paying patients to eye-care providers, though frequency limits and the $200 contact-lens cap would keep the benefit modest.

Many Medicare Advantage plans offer limited dental, vision, and hearing extras as a selling point; a universal Medicare benefit would erase that advantage while leaving their role intact. In this bill's death, their differentiator survives.
A 90% federal matching rate for adult dental, vision, and hearing services would shift most of the cost of covering those services from states to the federal government.
